title: Chips that touch the real world
summary: Sensors, amplifiers, converters and power chips: catch a heartbeat or a voice on a battery budget, and feed a chip without wasting power.

then: Analog chips such as the 741 op-amp (1968) amplify signals; most measuring still uses many separate parts.
Single-chip converters and switching regulators spread through instruments and computers.
Phones gather radio, audio converters and power management onto a few mixed-signal chips.
Smartphones fill with tiny motion sensors (MEMS) and camera sensors made on chip processes.
Always-on sensing: chips that listen for a wake word or count steps on microwatts.
Projection: more sensing moves next to the sensor, so only results, not raw samples, are sent.

learn.plain: A chip can only count. Analog chips are its senses and its food: a sensor turns light, sound or warmth into a tiny voltage, an amplifier makes it bigger, and a converter measures it again and again and writes each measurement as a number. Another chip turns the battery's voltage into the steady, lower voltage every other chip needs. Measuring more often and more finely gives a truer picture, but every number costs energy.
learn.engineer: The chain is sensor, low-noise amplifier, anti-alias filter, ADC and then processing or a radio. Sample above twice the highest frequency of interest (Nyquist), and use gain to fill the converter's range without clipping. ADC energy per sample scales roughly as FOM · 2^ENOB, and the radio's energy per bit often dominates, so low-power designs keep only the bits they need and process near the sensor. Power: an LDO's efficiency is about Vout/Vin and it is quiet; a buck converter reaches 85–95% at moderate loads but adds switching ripple and needs an inductor. Analog and power circuits gain little from new nodes, so they are made on mature processes. The model here leaves out filters, compression, duty cycling and real regulators' light-load modes.

quiz.q: A vibration has an important tone at 1,200 Hz. What is the slowest sampling rate that can still show it?
options: Any rate works if you use more bits
quiz.why: You need more than two samples per cycle of the fastest part (Nyquist). Sampling slower folds the tone into a false, slower one.

quiz.q: Why does a phone use a switching regulator rather than a linear one for its processor?
options: A linear regulator would turn most of the battery's power into heat when stepping 3.8 V down to 0.8 V
Linear regulators cannot supply more than 1 mA
quiz.why: A linear regulator's efficiency is about Vout/Vin, here about 21%; the rest is heat. A buck converter wastes far less.

quiz.q: Why are most analog and power chips made on older processes?
options: Nobody has designed them for new processes yet
Precise analog needs large, matched transistors and power chips need higher voltages, so shrinking helps little
quiz.why: Digital logic gains from every shrink; analog precision and voltage tolerance do not, so the cheaper mature process wins.
